items.question: How do you think about your OpenAI research team's role in developing new ways for people to interact with reasoning models?
items.object: The role of Karina Nguyen’s research team at OpenAI
items.answer:
Over time, I was trying to refine what my team is, and I feel like it's at an intersection of human-computer interaction, defining what the next interaction paradigms might look like with some of the most recent reasoning models, as well as actually trying to come up with novel methods to improve those models for certain tasks.

For Canvas, one of the most common use cases is writing and coding, and we're continually working on how do we make Canvas coding go beyond what is possible right now. That requires us to do our own training and come up with new methods of synthetic data generation. The way I'm thinking about it is that my team is going from full stack, from training models all the way up to deployment, and making sure that we create novel product features that are coherent to what ChatGPT can become.

items.question: How do you think about the potential and limitations of Claude operating inside Slack?
items.object: Claude operating inside Slack
items.answer:
The really first product that Anthropic built was Claude and Slack, and it shipped not long after. I still come back to that idea of Claude operating inside some of the organizational workplace like Slack. There's something magical in there.

I remember we built ideas like summarize the thread, but you can imagine having automated ways of maybe Claude should summarize multiple channels every week, custom for what you like or what you want. We built some really cool features like tag Claude, and then ask to summarize what happened in the thread, suggest new ideas. But we didn't quite double down because you could imagine Claude having access to the files or Google Drive that you can upload in, just connectors in Slack. Also, the UX was kind of constraining at that time. I was thinking, we wanted to do this feature, but Slack's interface constrained us, and we didn't want to be dependent on the platform, Slack.

items.question: Why do you think shared AI workspaces like Canvas could have happened earlier?
items.object: The timing and UX priorities behind Canvas-like AI workspaces
items.answer: Yeah, I come back to that question a lot. I was working on something similar to Canvas but for Claude at that time, in 2023. It was the same similar idea of a Claude workspace where a human and a Claude could have a shared workspace document. I think it kind of evolved. At that time, I was in the product engineering team, and then I switched to the research team. The product engineering team grew so much; they had their own ideas of Artifacts and Projects. Not necessarily that they looked at my previous explorations, but when I was exploring Claude documents or Claude workspace, I don't think anybody was thinking about UX as much, or many researchers understood that. Those ideas could have happened two years ago. Maybe it wasn't a priority at that time. The AI landscape was very nascent; nobody, even when I would talk to some of the designers at that time, product designers, they were not even thinking about that at all.

items.question: How do you think about detecting and fixing problems caused by data interactions during model training?
items.object: Data interactions and debugging during model training
items.answer: What I've learned is that you will end up with, I don't know, 70 models, and every model will have its own brain damage, kind of personality-wise or performance-wise. Every model is very different. One of the interesting research questions is how do you understand the data interactions as you train the model? If you train the model on contradictory datasets, how can you make sure that there won't be weird side effects? Sometimes you get side effects. The learning is that you have to iterate very rapidly, debug and detect it, and make interventions. Some of the techniques from software engineering are very useful here.

items.question: How do you reconcile taking chances on “YOLO” model-training runs with carefully prioritizing experiments?
items.object: Compute allocation and research management for model-training experiments
items.answer: Well, I think it's dependent on how much compute you have. It's actually a lot of questions in research on how do you most effectively use the compute that you have. Maybe you can have two to three runs that are only YOLO runs, but if you don't have that luxury, you need to prioritize ruthlessly what are the experiments that are most important to run. I think this is what research management is, basically: how do you fund efforts, prioritize, take research bets, and make sure that you build conviction in those bets rapidly, such that if they work out, you double down on them.

items.question: Why do you think it is so hard to have one standard way of evaluating different AI models?
items.object: Standardized evaluation across AI models
items.answer: I think it operates on an assumption that the next generation of the model, or the model that you produce next, is going to behave the same. The way you prompt o1 or Claude 3 is going to be very different from each other. There's a lot of prompting that you need to do to get the evals to run correctly. Sometimes a model would output new lines and the way it parses would be incorrect. This happened with Stanford HELM benchmarks. Somehow Claude was always not performing well, and that's because the way they prompted it was kind of wrong. It's a lot of techniques, and it's very hard because nobody even knows.

items.question: What have you found works well when you prompt o1?
items.object: Prompting o1 with hard constraints
items.answer: I actually think I did not even harness the magic of o1 prompting. One thing that I found is that if you give o1 hard constraints of what you're looking for, the model will have a much easier time to select the candidates and match the candidate that most fulfills the criteria that you gave. There's a class of problems like this that o1 excels at. For example, you might have a bio question, or, in chemistry, very specific criteria with the protein or some of the chemical bindings.

items.question: Why do you see alignment as especially important for complex reasoning models such as o1?
items.object: Human verification and alignment of complex reasoning models such as o1
items.answer: I think an interesting thing about o1 is that it's really for average humans. Sometimes I don't even know whether the model produced the correct output or not. It's really hard for me to verify even hard STEM questions. If I'm not an expert, I usually don't know. The question of alignment is actually more important for these complex reasoning models: how do we help humans verify the outputs of these models? That's quite important. items.question: How do you think about behavioral design for an AI model entering a collaborative context like ChatGPT Canvas?
items.object: Behavioral design for AI models in collaborative contexts
items.answer: I think behavioral design is really cool. I'm glad that I made it a section. Nobody had this term of behavioral design necessarily for the models. It's kind of a new little field of extending product design into model design. How do you create a behavior for the model in certain contexts? For example, in Canvas, one thing we had to think about is now the model enters a more collaborative environment, a collaborative context. What's the most appropriate behavior for the model to act like as a collaborator? Should it ask more follow-up questions? Should it change what's the tone should be? What is a collaborator tone? It's different from a chat conversationalist versus a collaborator. How do you shape the persona and the personality around that?

items.question: How do you approach designing an AI model's personality around core values that can conflict?
items.object: Designing model personalities around potentially conflicting core values
items.answer: I guess I can talk more about the methods of creating the personality. It's the same thing as you would create a character in a video game: charisma, intelligence, wisdom. What are the core principles, values? Obviously, for Claude it's much easier. It's baked in, the mission: honest, harmless, helpful. The most complicated thing about model behavior or behavioral design is that sometimes two values contradict each other. This happened in Claude 3. One of the main things we were thinking about is how do we balance honesty versus harmlessness or helpfulness? We don't want the model to always refuse, even to innocuous queries, some creative writing prompts, but we also don't want the model to act harmful. There's always a balance between those two, and it's more art than science. Data set crafting is more of an art than a literal science. You can definitely do empirical research on this, but this is the idea of synthetic data. If you look back to the Constitutional AI paper, it's about how do you create completions such that you would agree to certain principles that you want your model to agree on. If you create the core values of the model, how do you decompose those core values into specific scenarios? How does the model need to express its honesty in a variety of scenarios? This is where generalization happens when you craft the persona of the model.

items.question: How did you approach shaping the model behavior behind ChatGPT Canvas?
items.object: Post-training and the beta model strategy for ChatGPT Canvas
items.answer:
The idea is you can go that far with a prompted baseline. Prompted ChatGPT was the first thing we tried, Canvas as a tool. How do we define the behavior of Canvas? We found a bunch of different edge cases that we wanted to fix, and the only way to fix some of the edge cases is through post-training. What we did was retrain the entire 4o with our Canvas stuff. There are two reasons why we did this. First, we wanted to ship this as a beta model in the dropdown menu. We could rapidly iterate on user feedback as we ship it, and not go through the entire integration process into this new o1 model, which took some time. From beta to GA, it took, I think, three months. We wanted to ship our own model with that teacher to learn from user feedback very quickly.

With Canvas itself, we had a lot of behavioral questions: when does Canvas need to write comments, when does it need to update or edit the document, when does it need to rewrite the entire document versus edit a specific section the user asked for? I was also working on writing quality, so that was a perfect way for us to teach the model how to use Canvas and improve writing quality, if writing was one of the main use cases for ChatGPT.

items.question: How do you think about improving ChatGPT’s writing quality?
items.object: Improving ChatGPT’s writing quality
items.answer: I think of it in two directions. The first direction is how do you improve the quality of writing of the current use cases of ChatGPT? Most of the use cases are nonfiction writing, email writing, maybe blog posts, cover letters is one of the main use cases. The second one is how do we teach the model to literally think more creatively or write in a more creative manner, such that it will create novel forms of writing? The second one is a much longer-term research question, while the first one is more straightforward: we need to improve data quality for the writing use cases between the models.

items.question: How do you decide what counts as good writing when evaluating language models?
items.object: Evaluating writing quality in language models
items.answer: For evaluating writing quality, I worked with Jan's team on model design. They had a team of model writers, and we would work together. It's a human eval, internal human eval, on the prompt distribution that we cared about. We want to make sure the models that we used and trained were better. It was a more opinionated way of improving writing quality, because we worked with model designers to come up with principles of what makes this particular writing good. What makes email writing good? We had to craft a rubric on what makes it good, and during the eval we check the marks on this rubric.

items.answer: I think there's always a difference in model quality. The original better model that we released with Canvas was much more creative than even right now when I use 4o with Canvas. items.question: How do you think about ChatGPT Canvas as an interface for both writing and coding?
items.object: ChatGPT Canvas as an interface for writing and coding
items.answer: Canvas is kind of an IDE for both. I feel like this is where I'm coming from: ChatGPT evolves into this blank interface which can morph itself into whatever you're trying. The model should derive your true intent and modify the interface based on your intent. If you're writing, it should become the most powerful writing IDE possible; if it's coding, it should become a coding IDE. It's a little bit of an odd decision for me to call those two things the same product name, because they're basically two different UIs.

items.question: What do you find hardest about developing new AI product features such as ChatGPT Canvas?
items.object: Developing and evaluating new AI product features such as ChatGPT Canvas
items.answer:
It's always hard with any new product feature, like Canvas or Tasks or any other new features: you don't know how people would use this feature, so how do you even build evaluations that would simulate how people would use this feature? It's really hard for us. Therefore we try to lean on iterative deployment in order to learn from user feedback as much as possible.

We didn't know code edits was very difficult for a model. Do we go back to fundamentally improve code edits as a model capability, or do a workaround where the model will just rewrite the entire document, which yielded higher accuracy? Those are decisions we had to make: how do you improve the bar to the product quality but also make sure the model quality is part of it? This new way of product development is more like product research, model training, and product development going hand in hand. This is one of the hardest things, defining the entire model behavior. There are so many edge cases that might happen, especially when you do Canvas with other tools, like Canvas plus DALL-E, Canvas plus search. If you select a certain section and ask for search, how do you build such evals? What features or behaviors do you care the most about? This is how you build evals.

items.answer: Prototype, I would say, was a prompted baseline. Everything starts with a prompted baseline. items.question: How do you think collaboration with AI agents should build toward trusting them with delegated tasks?
items.object: Collaboration as a path to trustworthy AI agent delegation
items.answer:
I'm not sure if this is my definition of agents, but I feel like it's more how I think it makes sense. For me to trust an agent with my passwords or my credit card, I actually need to build trust with that agent, that it will handle my tasks correctly and reliably. The way I would go about this is how I would naturally collaborate with other people. At the beginning of any project, when we first meet, we don't know each other or each other's working style, what I prefer, what they prefer, how they prefer to communicate, et cetera. You spend the first two weeks just learning their style of working, and over time you adapt to their working style. This is how you create collaboration.

At the beginning you don't have much trust, so how do you build more trust? It's the same thing as with a manager: how do you build trust with your manager? What do they need to know about you? What do you need to know about them? Over time, as you build trust—and trust builds through collaboration. That's why I feel like building Canvas was kind of the first steps toward more collaborative agents. With humans, you need to show consistent effort to each other, that you care about each other and work together very well. Consistency and collaboration create trust. Then I will naturally try to delegate tasks to a model because I know the model will not fail me. It builds out the intuition for the form factor of new agents.

Sometimes researchers or people in the community are so into, "Yeah, agents, delegate everything," but on the way toward that, collaboration is one of the main roadblocks or milestones to get over, because then you will learn some of the implicit preferences that would help toward this full delegation model.
